one_line: Navan's chief architect and a colleague argue agent infrastructure is repeating the microservices shift: skills as context units, hook-based tracing, trajectory evals, and tool-call guardrails.
summary: Roberto Milev and Uday Kanagala from Navan (travel and expense management, AWS shop) compare the current agent stack to the 2015 microservices wave and say a reference architecture is forming. They say runtime and scaling are largely solved, with AWS AgentCore used plus their own session persistence and rehydration. For context, they treat skills as composable units that carry both instructions and tool execution, loaded with progressive disclosure. For observability, they say logs fail for long agents, so they intercept pre/post tool and session hooks to emit OpenTelemetry traces that capture goal, reasoning, belief, tool calls and a confidence signal. For evaluation, they use trajectory evals that measure progress from start to goal, since agents do not follow a fixed graph. For security, they run guardrails before and after every tool call and argue that agents acting on a user's behalf need fine-grained authorization. They prefer a single master agent with sub-skills over multi-agent systems, and use A2A for contracts across team boundaries. They end by listing observability, cost control, replay/debugging and standards as still open.

key_ideas.idea: Analogy to microservices: a reference architecture is forming for agents, and the advice carries over. If you cannot build a well-structured single agentic loop, a multi-agent system will not help.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker frames today's agent layers (runtime, memory, context, observability, guardrails, orchestration) as crystallizing the way microservices layers did, and says the time to learn them is measured in years.

key_ideas.idea: Agents are stateful, unlike stateless services, so the runtime needs persistent sessions, isolation and a different lifecycle. Navan uses AWS AgentCore but built session persistence and rehydration on top of it.
key_ideas.detail: Cloud runtimes are usually framework-agnostic but favor their own framework. The speaker says runtime and scaling are largely solved because LLM calls can be scaled brute force.

key_ideas.idea: Treat a skill as a unit of context: it holds domain instructions plus the tool execution the agent performs. Compose context dynamically from skills that are pluggable, testable alone and reusable.
key_ideas.detail: Progressive disclosure keeps the starting context small, with only metadata loaded at first, and expands later. The speaker says this works better than stuffing in more context, since agents lose focus when context is too large.

key_ideas.idea: Logs stop being the main debugging tool once agents run 20 to 30 steps. Hooks on pre/post tool calls and on session start and end let you intercept actions, block them, and emit OpenTelemetry traces.
key_ideas.detail: The traces should carry the current goal, the reasons for each action, the belief state and the tool calls. The speaker calls this a day-two operations problem.

key_ideas.idea: Attach a confidence signal to decisions, marking whether an answer is evidenced or inferred. Inferred answers go to a human in the loop, and the feedback helps classify regressions.
key_ideas.detail: The confidence signal records whether several paths led to the choice or whether the answer was inferred. The speaker says this gives reviewers a reason to look.

key_ideas.idea: Since agents are non-deterministic, judge them by trajectory rather than by a fixed expected flow. Measure how far the run progressed from start toward the goal, to score efficiency and completeness.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker says they rely heavily on trajectory evals, based on research papers, and combine them with the inferred-answer signal to catch regressions after changes.

key_ideas.idea: Guardrails and authorization must be applied before and after every tool call. An agent acting on a user's behalf blurs the line between user and service account, so authorization has to be fine-grained.
key_ideas.detail: Example given: an agent told to book a flight once the price drops below $200 is acting for the user, which raises the question of who made the purchase.

key_ideas.idea: Default to a single master agent that loads sub-skills and sub-agents progressively, not a multi-agent setup. Use A2A to define skill-level contracts across team boundaries when multiple agents are needed.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker calls single-versus-multi-agent an orchestration war and says Navan learned from failures that a single agent should be made to work first.

techniques.name: Pre/post tool-call and session hooks for tracing and gating
techniques.how: Intercept at pre-session, pre-tool, post-tool and post-session. At each point either block the action or emit a metric or OpenTelemetry span. Their agent setup used Claude Code hooks, with a provider tool (likely Braintrust, auto-caption 'brain trusts') for trace emission.
techniques.when: Long multi-step agent runs where you need to see where an agent got stuck, or where policy checks must run before each tool call.

techniques.name: Trace signals: goal, reasons, belief, tool calls, confidence
techniques.how: Record the current goal, the reasoning for each step, a belief status, the tool calls and a confidence score for each decision. Flag whether an answer was inferred or evidenced.
techniques.when: Reviewing failed or uncertain agent runs, and deciding when a human should step in.

techniques.name: Trajectory evaluation
techniques.how: Define a start and a goal, then measure how far the agent's actual path progressed along that route. Use the result as an efficiency and completeness score instead of matching an exact sequence of steps.
techniques.when: Evaluating non-deterministic, multi-step agents where any single correct path is acceptable.

techniques.name: Skills as composable, testable context units
techniques.how: Package each domain as a skill with its instructions and its tools. Load only the metadata first with progressive disclosure, then expand the skill when the task needs it. Compose a context per run from several skills.
techniques.when: Building domain-specific agents where a single large context degrades focus.

techniques.name: Single master agent with progressively loaded sub-skills
techniques.how: Run one agent that decides which sub-skills or sub-agents to load as the task unfolds, rather than starting several agents up front.
techniques.when: Before splitting work into multiple agents; use it as the default starting architecture.

techniques.name: Per-tool-call authorization for on-behalf-of agents
techniques.how: Run policy checks before and after each tool call, with fine-grained authorization that separates the user, the agent and the service account.
techniques.when: Enterprise agents that handle sensitive data or take actions with money or accounts for a user.

techniques.name: A2A skill contracts across team boundaries
techniques.how: Use the A2A protocol to expose skills as contracts between agents owned by different teams, so the boundary is an explicit interface.
techniques.when: Large organizations where separate teams build agents that need to call one another.

hot_takes: If you cannot build a well-structured single agentic loop, you should not try a multi-agent orchestrated system.
Logs are the wrong debugging tool for agents, which produce too much reasoning output to read by hand.
Agent cost is hard to predict, and the speaker thinks AI vendors benefit when customers spend more tokens.
Runtime and orchestration are largely solved, while observability, replay and standards are still open.

relevance.why: The talk's pre/post tool-call hooks, trace signals and trajectory evals map onto the L4 observability stack and the RAGAS eval setup, and per-tool-call guardrails match the Govrix Scout gateway checks.
ProsHarness wraps Claude Code and checkpoints long runs, and the talk's hook-based tracing shows where a stalled step can be recorded before a checkpoint resume.
relevance.action: Log the goal and each tool call through Claude Code hooks in ProsHarness, and record the step where a run stalls so a checkpoint resume can start from the right point.
